fullText:
The contract for a new plant in Baltimore is the latest linked to the brothers.

President Donald Trump announced a $6.6 billion investment with AI defense company Anduril Industries on Tuesday -- the most recent government funding agreement into a company with investment ties to the president's sons.

The Trump administration announced the Navy will support $2.9 billion of the total cost to help create a new facility in Baltimore County, Maryland, that will manufacture critical parts for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine.

"In a tremendous victory for our country and for the city of Baltimore, Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in a state-of-the-art shipyard that will be known forever as Arsenal-2," Trump said at an event announcing the investment.

"Right here in Sparrows Point, you'll build the next generation of American submarines, including autonomous subs, torpedo tubes, and critical components for our cutting edge Virginia-class attack submarines," Trump said.

1789 Capital -- a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders -- claimed a stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.

Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov, the official system for government contracting.

Anduril did not respond for comment on its contracts or investments from 1789 Capital, though the company has been awarded contracts dating back to 2019, according to USASpending.gov

The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one.

An ABC News analysis found defense companies backed by the president's sons, including Anduril, have now raked in more than $6 billion dollars in active or promised government contracts since those investments were made, according to the government's official contract reporting.

This comes as Congressional Oversight Democrats continue to demand the Pentagon's inspector general investigate the approved deals.

"Refusal to investigate these serious allegations will raise significant concerns about whether your office is able to perform its statutory duty as an independent watchdog over DoD," lawmakers Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, Robert Garcia and Tammy Duckworth wrote in a letter to Platte B. Moring, III, the Pentagon's inspector general, in May.

A Pentagon official told ABC News, "No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."

A spokesperson for the Trump brothers denied any wrongdoing.

"Don and Eric are experienced business leaders who have built and invested in businesses across a wide range of industries for decades, long before their father first ran for public office. Their investment decisions are based solely on their independent business judgment and personal convictions and they do not seek to influence, direct, or participate in any government decision, procurement, award, regulatory action, or other governmental process. Attempts to portray their ordinary investment activities as improper are a deliberate distortion of the facts," the spokesperson said.

The White House declined to comment.

Shortly after Trump won the presidency, Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for Florida-based drone manufacturer Unusual Machines -- a company which had not previously won any government contracts.

In October 2025, Unusual Machines scored a direct U.S. Dept. of Defense agreement for 3,500 orders of National Defense Authorization Act-compliant motors, with a potential order of 20,000 on the way in 2026.

The Trump brothers are also listed as "notable investors" for the U.S. drone company Powerus, the company announced in March 2026.

Despite not having any government contracts previously, Powerus won its first Air Force purchase order just one month later for an undisclosed amount.

In July, Powerus was awarded up to $90 million for aerial-denial unmanned aircraft systems from the U.S. Air Force.

ABC News asked Powerus if it was concerned at all about the involvement of the Trump brothers in the company, given its active contracts.

"Defense procurement is merit-based. You can't sell the government something that won't protect a soldier, and nobody in the procurement chain risks their career routing a contract to a company whose equipment doesn't work," a spokesperson for Powerus said.

"Neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company's day-to-day business," the spokesperson continued. "Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company."

Trump-linked investments extend into the manufacturing industry, with the brothers combining for more than $1 billion across companies in mining, quantum computing and aerospace.

Oversight Democrats in their letter to the DoD criticized Donald Trump Jr.'s portfolio in raw materials, citing an August 2025 investment into Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth mining company that harvests critical materials for defense manufacturing.

That same month, the Office of Strategic Capital loaned Vulcan Elements $620 million to expand its operation.

Vulcan Elements did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts and the investments from 1789 Capital.

The firm also invested $60 million in Texas-based Firehawk Aerospace, according to firm portfolios provided by PitchBook. In the same month, Firehawk won a $4.9 million Air Force contract to "Advance Hybrid Rocket Engine Development," according to a company press release.

Firehawk would later secure tens of millions more -- $3.2 million in May 2026, an undisclosed "multimillion-dollar" contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory in July and $24 million in Dept. of Defense munitions contracts in August, according to company press releases and active contracts.

Firehawk Aerospace has been awarded government contracts across both the Biden and Trump administrations since the company's founding in 2019.

In a statement to ABC News, Firehawk said its award is "solely the product of engineering expertise and capacity."

"We value the many investors who back that mission and share our conviction that the Nation's arsenal must be built to last. Our focus is the duty in front of us, making the arsenal of the U.S. and our allies stronger," a Firehawk spokesperson said.

ABC News also found 1789 Capital raised $1 billion in revenue generation for California-based PsiQuantum in September of last year, with the company's pre-existing contract with DoD expanding by more than $157 million since then, according to SAM.gov.

PsiQuantum also signed a $100 million letter of intent with the Department of Commerce and another $125 million with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency in May and July of 2026.

PsiQuantum did not respond when asked for comment on these investments.

Trump-linked investments were found in the automation sector.

Eric Trump said he was named chief strategy adviser for Foundation Future Industries, a humanoid robot startup with the stated aim to develop autonomous soldiers and workers.

Eric Trump touted a $24 million contract in April -- the company's first -- according to Eric Trump and CEO Sankaet Pathal's statements on Fox News. Pathal did not respond for comment on this contract or on Trump's involvement with the company's operations.

ABC News found a $391 million 1789 Capital investment into Hadrian -- a highly automated, AI-driven manufacturing company -- in the early days of 2026.

The company won its first public contracts a few months later in March -- a $39.2 million agreement with the Army for machinery and manufacturing and a $900 million deal with the Navy to create highly automated submarine factories.

Hadrian did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts.

Congressional Democrats continue to sound the alarm over these investments, referring ABC News to their May demand to the Department of Defense to launch an investigation into the president's family.

"We hope that your office will take seriously these latest concerns about corruption in the DoD award process and fulfill your statutory responsibility by initiating a review," the lawmakers wrote in their letter.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln a high-level award during a visit to the aircraft carrier Wednesday, a day before the ship returns home to San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war.

The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat, was bestowed upon the Lincoln and accompanying ships for "40 days of combat operations and an ironclad maritime blockade against Iran in support of Operation Epic Fury," Hegseth said, referring to the Trump administration's code name for the Iran war.

The carrier endured a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea, and its extended deployment drew national attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. After more than 10 months deployed, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Hegseth, who flew out to the ship before its arrival Thursday in San Diego, acknowledged to the crew that "I'm the only thing standing between you and home" and that his intention was "once they pull up to the dock, we're getting out of the way."

Long deployments can tax service members who are away from their families for extended periods while facing threats, and can add wear to the aircraft carriers, which have been used for President Donald Trump's military operations in the Middle East and South America.

The Lincoln is the second carrier that has endured an unusually long and arduous deployment to support the war against Iran and the second to receive the top unit award afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

As for the Lincoln, it departed San Diego in late November, arrived in the Middle East in January and now will be back in its home port.

Hegseth said Wednesday that Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The Navy initially played down early reports of supply problems on Lincoln and Trump said its lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough," Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

Navy officials also said that while combat operations led to delays in scheduled resupply shipments, they prioritized the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.

More recently, the service told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide while on the long deployment. Experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

According to the award that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and the strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

There are now two aircraft carriers assigned to the Middle East. The USS George Washington, though usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August.

The other aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could join the Washington and the Bush as early as the end of October.

title: Rays beat Yankees 5-2 to take 2-0 ALDS lead
description: (AP) — Richie Palacios hit a two-run single in a four-run fifth inning and the Tampa Bay Rays took advantage of New York’s sloppy defense, beating Cam Schlittler and the Yankees 5-2 on Monday night to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.The Rays are one victory from reaching the American League Championship Series.
fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Richie Palacios hit a two-run single in a four-run fifth inning and the Tampa Bay Rays took advantage of New York's sloppy defense, beating Cam Schlittler and the Yankees 5-2 on Monday night to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.

The Rays are one victory from reaching the American League Championship Series. Game 3 in the best-of-five playoff is Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.

Ben Rice hit a pair of homers for the Yankees, who are on the verge of elimination — which would extend their World Series drought to 17 seasons. They were dominated by Drew Rasmussen in the series opener and have scored just two runs in two games with three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge out of the lineup due to a calf injury.

The small-ball Rays chased Schlittler, the likely AL Cy Young Award winner, in the fifth aided by New York's defensive miscues.

Jonathan Aranda lined a single to start the inning and Junior Caminero ripped a double to right-center. With the infield drawn-in except second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was standing several feet further back on the dirt, Liam Hicks hit a bouncer to second that scored Aranda for a 2-1 lead. Chisholm's only play was at first because he wasn't all the way in like the rest of the infielders.

Chandler Simpson then hit a grounder that shortstop George Lombard Jr. booted, scoring Caminero to make it 3-1. It was initially ruled a hit and then changed to an error and eventually a fielder's choice. Brent Headrick replaced Schlittler and struck out Victor Mesa Jr. After Simpson stole second, Jonny DeLuca reached on a grounder when Lombard's throw to first was wide for New York's fourth error.

Palacios followed with a hard single to center that increased Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1.

That was plenty of support for one of the best bullpens in the majors.

Freddy Peralta allowed one run and three hits in 4 2/3 innings, Cam Booser pitched out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth and Ian Seymour gave up one run on Rice's solo shot in three innings. Bryan Baker finished with a perfect ninth for his second save in two games.

Schlittler, who was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA and dominated Boston in the opener of the wild-card round, lasted 4 1/3 innings. He allowed four runs — two earned — and six hits. Schlittler only fanned two.

CLEVELAND (AP) — Braden Montgomery lined a two-run double down the right-field line, Sean Burke allowed one hit in 5 1/3 innings of splendid relief and Chicago beat Cleveland to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.

The surprising White Sox improved to 4-0 in these playoffs — all on the road — and are one win from advancing to the American League Championship Series for the first time since winning the World Series in 2005. Chicago became the first team to reach the postseason after three straight 100-loss seasons, including a post-1900 record 121 defeats in 2024.

Jo Adell hit an RBI triple in the eighth and Chase DeLauter had two hits for the Guardians.

Starting pitcher Gavin Williams struck out 11, tied for second-most in a Cleveland postseason game. But the offense failed to produce for the second straight game.

Grant Taylor worked 1 1/3 innings and allowed one hit as he got his second straight save.

The best-of-five series shifts to Chicago for Game 3 on Wednesday.

title: Disastrous defense sinks Yankees in ALDS Game 2 loss to Rays
description: For the second time in three years, the Yankees had a disastrous defensive game in the postseason and it cost them again, this time in a 5-2 loss to the Rays Monday night in Game 2 of the AL Division Series.
fullText:
For the second time in three years, the Yankees had a disastrous defensive game in the postseason and it cost them again, this time in a 5-2 loss to the Rays Monday night in Game 2 of the AL Division Series.

The Yanks made four errors in the loss, leading to three unearned runs, and they now teeter on the brink of elimination, down two games to none in the best-of-five series. Game 3 is set for Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.

Two years ago, the Yankee defense collapsed in Game 5 of the World Series against the Dodgers and they were eliminated. But even that game only featured three Yankee errors – in the box score, anyway.

Monday's debacle was only the fifth time the Yankees have made four errors in a single postseason game. The last time was in the 2019 ALCS against the Astros.

The Yankees have scored only twice so far in the series, on two solo home runs by Ben Rice Monday night. No Aaron Judge, who is out with a calf injury, certainly doesn't help.

-- Yankee starter Cam Schlittler was not nearly as brilliant as he's been in his previous postseason outings. He lasted just 4.1 innings and allowed seven hits and four runs (only two earned). He struck out just two and didn't have a strikeout until the fourth inning and got only seven swings-and-misses. He also walked one. His career postseason ERA rose from 0.87 to 1.44.

-- The Yankees defensive implosion started in the very first inning and set a dubious club record for errors in a single postseason frame – three. The Yankees had never had three errors in one October inning and this is the 61st postseason appearance in the Yankees' existence. The Yanks last committed three errors in an inning in any game on Aug. 21, 2025 against the Red Sox. The last time it happened in any postseason game was Game 5 of the 2015 ALDS when the Rangers did it in a loss to the Blue Jays.

-- Ryan McMahon, who has a fine defensive reputation, though he has not had his best season with the glove, made the first miscue when the leadoff hitter, Yandy Díaz, hit a topspin bouncer to him that McMahon muffed. Jonathan Aranda followed with a single and then Junior Caminero hit what could've been a double-play grounder to short. George Lombard Jr. made a not-that-graceful flip to the bag and Jazz Chisholm Jr. grabbed it and threw wildly to first. Díaz scored and Caminero went to second.

Then it seemed like Schlittler had Hicks struck out, but, upon replay review, Austin Wells was called for catcher's interference – his mitt was clearly in the path of Hicks' bat. That was the third error of the inning. They nearly had a fourth – Chisholm fielded Simpson's grounder but threw high to second base, pulling Lombard off the bag. But Lombard got back in time for a force out. Schlittler got a grounder from Victor Mesa to mercifully end the inning. The Yankees only allowed one run, but all the gaffes forced Schlittler to endure some tense moments and extra pitches.

-- The Rays scored four runs in the fifth inning and knocked out Schlittler. They got some weak contact and used their speed to exploit it. Poor Yankee defense helped, too. Aranda started the inning with a single and Caminero followed with a ringing double. With the infield mostly in – Chisholm was further back than the rest of the infielders – Liam Hicks hit a grounder that was slow enough to allow Aranda to score.

Chandler Simpson later hit a soft grounder to short that Lombard couldn't backhand and another run scored. The scoring on that play was changed several times, but it was ultimately scored an infield single. But Lombard then made a throwing error to further prolong the inning and Richie Palacios added a single after an eight-pitch bout with reliever Brent Headrick that scored two more runs.

-- The Yanks went nine up, nine down the first time through their batting order as Rays starter Freddy Peralta looked sharp. But Rice tied the score at 1 with a 372-foot drive over the right-field fence. Rice connected on the fourth of four consecutive changeups from Peralta. Rice also homered in the eighth inning, giving him four home runs in four games this postseason.

-- In the fifth, the Yanks had a big chance with two outs, but could not cash in. Wells lashed a double into the right-field corner that looked a lot like the ball he hit in Game 1 and got thrown out trying to stretch into a triple. He wisely stopped at second this time. McMahon then worked a walk in a tough, seven-pitch at-bat. He was the last batter that Peralta faced. He came out with Rice coming up to the plate.

Rice worked another walk against southpaw Cam Booser, which brought up Cody Bellinger, who was 11th in MLB with a .340 average with runners in scoring position. Bellinger hit a deep fly ball to the warning track in center that held some hope, but it was caught.

-- Peralta, the former Met who got his pitching together in Tampa Bay, lasted 4.2 innings and allowed one run and three hits. He struck out three and walked one. The outing lowered his career postseason ERA from 4.32 to 4.03.

title: Sen. Tillis calls deciding vote for Hegseth the 'biggest regret' of his career
description:
— Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. 
In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term.

In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations.

"I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far."

He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say."

Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically.

Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent."

At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass."

Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections.

"All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes.

The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way."

Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie.

On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result."

On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor.

"I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes.

If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape."

He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his " Big Beautiful Bill " of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done."

"Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes.

He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT."

In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults.

Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response.

"I care if you fail and right now we are failing," Tillis wrote to Trump.

title: Aidan Hutchinson Sends Blunt Message to Fans Amid Lions Struggles

fullText:
The Detroit Lions defense is the worst in the NFL through four weeks. While star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is having a good season, he is the leader of this unit and is taking accountability for the struggles.

Hutchinson was asked what can be said by him and his teammates, not only in the locker room, but to the frustrated fans. The Lions' four-year, $180M star edge rusher made it clear that nothing can be said right now because talk is cheap."

"I'm so tired of talk," declared Hutchinson on the discussions going on in the locker room. "To me, talk is cheap. If you really want to do something, let's go win the damn game and make the plays we need to make."

Hutchinson was fired up when discussing what the team needs to do.

However, when he was asked what the team can do on paper, or within the scheme, to change things, he admitted that he is just as stumped as defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard.

"I'm not sure right now," admitted Hutchinson. "I'm kind of still analyzing and trying to figure out what is going wrong."

However, Hutchinson made it clear to fans that he is not quitting on the team despite the slow start. He still sees things turning around and the team making the most of this.

"I'm going to stay in it," said Hutchinson. "I am going to keep improving individually and try to do anything I can do to help our team win."

The Lions star told fans not to quit and to stay in it with him. He noted that he sees a semblance of a dangerous team. They just need to put everything together.

"I know we're going to figure it out," said Hutchinson. "And when we do, when we're clicking on all cylinders, we're going to be such a dangerous team."

Detroit is still 2-2 despite the defense. If they can get the defense figured out, the offense is going to help them win games.

The Lions' secondary gets a lot of the bad reputation on the defense, and that is rightfully so. However, the edge rusher group outside of Hutchinson is also a disappointment.

Hutchinson has 29 pressures on 182 pass rush snaps. He has a 27.1% win rate and a 9.9 pass-rush productivity rate per PFF. D.J. Wonnum is second on the team with eight pressures on 128 pass-rush snaps.

He has a 4.7 PRP and an 11% win rate. Tyler Lacy has 51 pass rush snaps and a 3.1 PRP, with a 6.3% win rate. Lastly is rookie Derrick Moore. The second-round pick has just 29 pass rush snaps. Moore has three pressures and a 5.4 PRP. He has a disappointing 3.6% pass-rush win rate.

The secondary is a problem, but the three rushers behind Hutchinson have not carried their weight. Hutchinson can only do so much. The others need to step up.

fullText:
TOKYO (AP) — The arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has drawn condemnation from Japan's leaders and renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island.

The alleged killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to strengthen Japanese military defense on the island and to work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China in the region.

Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.

Security camera footage showed a man wearing a black top, trousers and white sneakers entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.

Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.

"I'm outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder," Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times.

People in Okinawa have long been wary of the U.S. presence on the island but many have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today.

There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.

After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime.

About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, condemning the crime and renewing demands that U.S. military bases be removed from the island.

One sign read: "We've had enough of this!"

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."

Koja said the case underscored the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes.

"I'm enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident," Koja told Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General in Naha, Andrew Ou on Monday when he summoned them to the prefectural government. He demanded that U.S. officials take effective preventive measures.

Watson replied: "I recognize the serious incident caused significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbors" and that "we are committed to being good neighbors … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people."

In Tokyo, Takaichi condemned the crime and demanded full cooperation and tougher disciplinary and preventive measures by the United States.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also summoned U.S. Forces Japan Commander Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost to his ministry, while Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi expressed his outrage to the U.S. ambassador to Japan, George Glass.

Glass, on X, expressed his condolences Sunday to the victim's family and said the United States is cooperating with Japanese authorities.

On Monday, he said he is telling U.S. military commanders of the need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity" and that he and Watson discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."

Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.

Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks.

If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

fullText:
Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll has given his first interview since resigning from the Pentagon in September after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Driscoll is just one of a series of high profile departures since Hegseth took over, with the secretary carrying out a purge so substantial it reportedly even raised President Donald Trump’s concerns.

Speaking to Rolling Stone, Driscoll acknowledged the pair had disagreements on a number of issues, without going into specifics.

“Once he makes a decision, there’s nothing I can do about it. I don’t have to like it,” he said of Hegseth. “But I think it’s unfair to describe our relationship so flatly – that every interaction was bad, or that we disagreed on everything.

“If you polled us, we probably agreed on more than 50 percent of things. What’s been reported is all the things we disagree on.

“I’ll never talk about our private conversations but we were both very passionate about our positions, and I would advocate as strongly as I possibly could – knowing I’m talking to my boss, and the final decision-maker.”

Driscoll said his role had been “to advocate as hard as I could for leaders who I thought were good.”

An Iraq War veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance – whom he befriended while they were contemporaries at Yale Law School – Driscoll is characterized in the piece as a keen modernizer of the U.S. military, interested in innovation and ensuring the Armed Forces had the equipment necessary to meet the challenges of a 21st century battlefield.

While Hegseth was also interested in making changes to the operation of the military, reports suggest he has been concerned about instilling a “warfighter” mentality in the troops and focussing on appearance.

Driscoll, the youngest person ever to hold his position after sailing through his confirmation hearing in the Senate in February 2025, recounts how he approached Hegseth early on with what he considered a “gift” – his close friendship with Vance – which he believed would help the Pentagon get what it needed from the White House.

But, the magazine reported: “Hegseth blew up at him… telling Driscoll that he needed to go through his office before reaching out to the White House, creating a tension between the two men.”

The friction worsened as Hegseth dismissed more and more top generals and admirals, culminating in the removal of Gen. Randy George and then Gen. Christopher Donahue, two men with whom Driscoll had found common cause in pursuing his modernizing agenda.

Driscoll reached the end of his tether in late August and informed President Donald Trump of his intention to resign, reportedly telling the commander-in-chief that he was leaving because Hegseth had fired everyone working towards the goal he held dear.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, responded to The Independent’s inquiry about Driscoll’s comments by calling Rolling Stone “a fake news rag regurgitating months-old false narratives in an attempt to stay relevant to their ever-dwindling audience” and alleging that its interview “is riddled with made-up claims regarding Secretary Hegseth’s historic achievements and transformative leadership.”

“Since Day One, Secretary Hegseth has focused on modernization across every branch of our Armed Forces and has moved with urgency to deliver on President Trump’s vision of Peace Through Strength,” Parnell said.

“From slashing bureaucracy, to untying the hands of our warfighters, to re-energizing our defense industrial base, Secretary Hegseth has been a generational Secretary for the Pentagon. With President Trump and Secretary Hegseth at the helm, our military will remain the greatest fighting force on the planet.”

Driscoll was praised by White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly when he left his post as “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more.”

"The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

title: Who is Michele Tafoya? Ex-sideline reporter aims to turn Minnesota red in Senate race.
description:
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion’s share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers. 
Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red.
fullText:
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion's share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers.

Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red.

In pursuit of that goal, the GOP has put its hopes in Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and NFL sideline reporter turned politician who polls suggest has a real chance of winning in a state that has been dominated by Democrats in recent election cycles.

Tafoya is running for the seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not pursuing re-election. Instead her opponent will be Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan, a progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Minnesota has been at the center of some of the biggest controversies of President Trump's second term, particularly his administration's sweeping immigration crackdown. Though a majority of Minnesotans disapprove of Trump's performance as president, Tafoya has steadily chipped away at Flanagan's lead in polls since the primary.

Here's what you need to know about who she is, what she stands for and how she went from the sidelines to the center of one of the midterms' most pivotal races.

Tafoya was born and raised in Southern California. Her father was an aeronautical engineer, and her mother was a school teacher. She has Hispanic heritage on her father's side.

She married her husband, Mark Vandersall, in 2000. They have two children. Tafoya has been open about her struggles with infertility, which included several miscarriages. Her daughter, Oliva, was adopted from Colombia as a nod to her father's lineage.

After launching her sports broadcasting career in Los Angeles, she moved to Minnesota in the early 1990s to take a job at the KFAN sports radio station in Minneapolis. Before long, she moved on to a national role with CBS, which proved to be the jumping-off point for a decades-long career that made her one of the country's most recognizable sports broadcasters. She covered five Super Bowls, the NBA and the Olympics — winning five Emmys for her work along the way.

Tafoya's last broadcast was during Super Bowl LVI in 2022. Her political career began the very next day. Less than 12 hours after the game ended, she announced that she would co-chair the campaign of Republican Kendall Qualls in his bid to become Minnesota governor.

Tafoya has said she always had strong political views, but made a specific effort to keep them out of her work as a broadcaster.

"I was not as free to be as vocal about world events that I'm concerned about," she told The Athletic in 2022. "It's not because I was told to shut up. I want to be very clear about that. But look, if you're on a show like Sunday Night Football … the last thing they want to do is invite controversy."

Tafoya was more open about her beliefs outside on social media, where she would regularly promote work from conservative outlets. But she also made statements that broke from the GOP mainstream, including support for efforts to curb climate change. In an interview with Sports Illustrated in 2015, she described herself as a "pro-choice" conservative with "definite libertarian strains."

After retiring from broadcasting, Tafoya made several appearances as a speaker at Republican political events, including the Conservative Political Action Conference. She was also a guest host on The View, taking on the role of the conservative-leaning voice in contrast to the show's more liberal regular panelists.

In 2022, Tafoya launched a podcast that frequently touched on political topics and featured Republican politicians as guests. The most recent episode, released in January, includes an interview with former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell, who unsuccessfully ran for Minnesota governor this year despite an endorsement from President Trump.

Tafoya formally announced her Senate bid a few weeks later. In August, she comfortably won a crowded Republican primary to set up a head-to-head race against Flanagan in November.

In her pitch to Minnesota voters, Tafoya has leaned into her sports background.

"I'm not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer," she said while standing on a snow-covered football field in her campaign announcement video.

For years, I walked the sidelines when the stakes were the highest, and that job taught me how leadership really works.I'm running for U.S. Senate to bring that experience to Washington and deliver the real results Minnesota deserves. https://t.co/vDbHWpAXg9

— Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) January 21, 2026

Like other swing-state Republicans across the country, Tafoya has worked to find a balance between supporting Trump and pushing back on some of his most unpopular policies.

She has supported the president throughout the war with Iran, at one point telling Minnesotans to "take one less trip to Starbucks" to help offset the rising cost of gas. More recently, though, she has joined a growing list of GOP candidates who have called for Trump to end the conflict.

"No president of either party should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people. That includes President Donald Trump," Tafoya told Twin Cities local news KSTP on Saturday.

Tafoya added that she would be "inclined to vote to end this war" if given the opportunity in the Senate. She has also said she didn't agree with ICE's tactics in Minneapolis and described Trump's tariff policies as "hit or miss."

Her policy views mostly align with mainstream Republican positions. She backs strong immigration enforcement and Trump's mass deportation campaign, a "tough on crime" approach to public safety, tax cuts, and laws barring transgender athletes from competing in women's and girls' sports. On abortion, she says she agrees with the Supreme Court's decision overturning Roe v. Wade, but personally believes there should be "reasonable access" in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

Tafoya's own opinions of Trump have evolved as well. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Trump not to run for a second term, describing his previous time in the White House as "absolute mayhem." She also said on her podcast around the same time that there was much about Trump that she found "difficult to accept."

But during the 2024 presidential campaign, Tafoya said she was supporting Trump with "more enthusiasm" than before. She also said she felt "sort of agnostic" on the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. She celebrated Trump's victory later that year, describing it as "morning in America" — a reference to Ronald Reagan's famous phrase from the 1980s.

Tafoya has mostly left Trump out of her current campaign ads and speeches, instead focusing her messaging on issues like fraud, affordability and public safety. The president opted not to endorse a candidate in Minnesota's Republican primary and has yet to throw his support behind Tafoya in the general election.

Tafoya is one of the few Republicans in major races across the country who is outperforming expectations in the polls.

title: CounterSteer: Suppressing Indirect Prompt Injection with Activation Steering
description: Indirect prompt injection makes an LLM agent treat untrusted retrieved text as instructions. We present CounterSteer, an inference-time defense that suppresses this behavior inside the model. Per model, a five-step recipe fits a residual-stream direction from paired episodes differing only in whether an embedded instruction is followed, and retains it only if it passes pre-specified causal and capability gates. At deployment, the direction is subtracted from every tool-result token during prefill. The edit is always on--there is no detection decision to evade--and requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary model, or added tokens, only white-box serving and tool-result span boundaries.

fullText:
There were three changes to the BVB women's starting XI compared to the previous week: Lara Schmidt came into central defense for Melanie Schuster, Noreen Günnewig replaced Ricarda Walkling in midfield, and Lena Ostermeier started in place of Ann-Sophie Vogel, who came on at halftime.

Playing in their usual 4-3-3 formation, the BVB women took to the well-kept artificial pitch in Cologne in summery temperatures. The hosts from the cathedral city started boldly, testing the black-and-yellows' defensive shape early on and giving Laura van der Laan her first task in the seventh minute. The BVB goalkeeper had to come off her line decisively to clear the danger.

At the other end, the BVB women took the lead from their second corner of the game (12'). Rita Schumacher's delivery was headed home by Lara Schmidt for her third headed goal of the season.

With the lead behind them, the BVB women gained even more control of the game, enjoying increasing possession and creating further chances through Alex Popp (24') and Annika Enderle (28'). During a Cologne counterattack, it was Laura van der Laan again who successfully slid in to cut out a through ball in the 30th minute. On the counterattack that followed, Cologne goalkeeper Felicitas Müller took center stage by parrying Jacqueline Meißner's volley on the line. Further attacks in the first half failed to find the net, and the black-and-yellows went into the break with a 1–0 lead.

At the restart, head coach Markus Högner made a triple substitution: Ann-Sophie Vogel, Jenske Steenwijk, and Ronja Leubner were brought on to provide fresh attacking ideas. While the first efforts were blocked by Cologne's defense, a rebound fell to substitute Ronja Leubner in the 56th minute, and she fired home ruthlessly from eleven meters to make it 2–0. Shortly before that, Alex Popp had intercepted a goal kick from the Cologne goalkeeper and started the move with her cross into the box.

After that, the Borussia women pushed for more goals. Long-range efforts from Ostermeier (63') and a volley from Schumacher (70') either missed the target or were saved by the in-form goalkeeper. So it was once again a corner from Rita Schumacher that found its way into the opposition net via Lara Schmidt – 3–0 in the 71st minute.

Eight minutes later, Ann-Sophie Vogel broke through down the left wing. Her cross found Ronja Leubner, who did not make full contact with her shot and in doing so forced an own goal for 4–0.

Shortly before the end, Rita Schumacher capped off a run in behind with a goal of her own (84'), which also sealed the final score. That means the BVB women remain unbeaten at the top of the table after seven matchdays, ahead of Bayer 04 Leverkusen's also unbeaten U23s.

On matchday eight of the Regionalliga West, the BVB women host promoted Niederrheinliga side Rhenania Bottrop at Stadion Rote Erde. fullText:
A Russian drone struck a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the city to the sound of air raid sirens, explosions and air defense systems being activated.

Merz is in Kyiv to display support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid Russia’s escalation of strikes on the city.

“Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said.

Highlighting attacks on Ukraine’s towns, residential buildings and energy, he said: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn ⁠against us.”

Video footage from Sunday morning’s strike showed the moment the city’s Northern Bridge was attacked, sparking a huge plume of fire and black smoke while cars were still traveling across. Two people were injured, the city’s mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko said.

It is the second time the Northern Bridge has been hit in as many days. On Thursday and Friday, Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation and the city’s subway system, was hit five times in less than 24 hours.

Ukrainian officials have said that Russian strikes on the capital’s infrastructure are attempting to cut the capital into two, as Kyiv is split along the Dnipro River, with businesses offices and government institutions on the right back, and the left bank mostly residential.

Kyiv plans to start building several alternative crossings over the Dnipro in case the attacks on the bridges continue, the minister of infrastructure said Sunday.

Russia’s defense ministry said it struck the Northern Bridge on Sunday, saying that it was targeting a route used for transporting troops and military equipment. It added that two cargo vessels carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa were struck. On Saturday the Russian Ministry of Defense said that it also targeted a logistics center in the Kyiv region.

Merz visited Kyiv alongside his Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katarina Reiche, despite warnings from Russia on Saturday that foreign visitors and dignitaries to the Ukrainian capital are not safe amid an onslaught of Russian attacks.

Zelensky and Merz are tying up a significant defense and industrial partnership, which will see the two countries finalize a deal for the production of drones and missiles.

Berlin is also expected to release €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid and €350 million ($390 million) for repairs to Ukraine’s damaged energy infrastructure, German government officials said.

Zelensky has warned that Ukraine’s defensive need is expanding amid Russia’s accelerated air campaign, which has seen Moscow fire high-speed, jet-powered Shahed-type drones that can bypass some of Ukraine’s air defense systems and exploit its lack of interceptors.

Earlier on Sunday, Merz said that Ukraine “is facing decisive weeks ahead.” Writing on X, he said: “I have traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.”

Meanwhile, there appears to be no immediate respite for Kyiv’s three million residents, with Moscow on Sunday saying that it will only intensify its strikes targeting the capital and other cities.

“Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as associated infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said.

Russia’s renewed threat follows an interview Zelensky gave to Reuters news on Saturday, where he outlined that he plans to double down on attacks on oil refineries.

“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners, etc. – what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said.

His comments come despite the urging of US President Donald Trump, who recently asked Ukraine to stay away from attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure, claiming it was sending global oil prices surging.

CNN’s Kara Fox and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

title: Trump names Jay Clayton as AI czar: Where he stands on AI safety
description:
President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
fullText:
President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies.

Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a "morally binding" agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are "Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers."

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media. Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI.

"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month. "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."

According to the Guardian, Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March.

Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far.

Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management. (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe.

After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time. But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.

"I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States."

During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat."

"We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence" — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development.

"Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy."

Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check.

"My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard."

According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported.

Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'

"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job. "He's right here. That's a good idea."

It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force."

"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.

According to Axios, Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."

When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI. Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."

The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

title: Arizona State's third-down defense struggles mightily in Baylor loss
description: Baylor finished the game 9-for-15 on 3rd downs, with multiple explosive plays. The Bears had gains of 27 yards, 19 yards and 11 yards on third downs.
fullText:
Prior to the Baylor game, most of Arizona State's fans' complaints centered on the offensive side of the ball. Now, that attention is likely to turn to the defense.

ASU's defense had almost no answers for Baylor's offense, particularly on third down. That part of the defense hasn't been a concern for ASU under defensive coordinator Brian Ward, but it was exposed in the blowout 55-19 loss to Baylor on Oct. 3.

Baylor finished the game 9-for-15 on third downs, with multiple explosive plays. The Bears had gains of 27 yards, 19 yards and 11 yards on third downs, just in the first half alone. At one point, Baylor was 8-for-11 on third-down conversion attempts.

Coming into the game, ASU was allowing opponents to convert 30% of their third downs — tied for 27th in the NCAA. But that was nowhere to be seen against Baylor. The unit looked completely different.

With 9:29 left in the third quarter, ASU students started to file out of Mountain America Stadium in Tempe.

"We couldn't create a pass rush," coach Kenny Dillingham said. "If you can't create a pass rush — they were getting the ball downfield because you can't create a pass rush — you're not going to be good on third-down defense. Then, you gotta give them credit. They throw some nice back shoulders too. They made some plays on one-on-one situations."

Dillingham emphasized the need to create a pass rush and what his team is doing to start it.

"As a coaching staff, we gotta evaluate that, what we're doing to create a pass rush," he said. "You gotta impact the quarterback. He wasn't impacted in the game, got into a good rhythm. The wideouts were playing well, and they got into a rhythm with him."

ASU finished the game with two sacks and five quarterback hurries.

There were also plays of 63 yards, 32 yards, 25 yards, 17 yards and 15 yards, all coming in the first half as well. Missed tackles were left all over the field. There were wide-open holes for Baylor's offense, both in the running game and passing game. Baylor had 496 yards of offense by the end of the third quarter. The Bears finished the game with 564 yards.

It was part of a dismal night on defense for ASU, which allowed the most points in a game since the 59-23 loss to Arizona in 2023.

Linebacker Owen Long said it isn't on one person or position group.

"It just obviously wasn't good enough tonight," Long said. "Not a good feeling right now. I don't know exactly what to say specifically. I have to go back and watch the tape, but including myself and everyone else, we've got to find a way to get better. So it starts right after this, tomorrow. Just find a way to get better. We just have to get back to work and find exactly what's going on.

"But it's on everyone. It's not just one person. Everyone's got to do a little bit better. It's just feeling the vibe in the locker room already. We just have to find a way to keep getting better."

Was there any hangover from the long overseas trip to London two weeks ago, followed by the bye week? Maybe. ASU's journey to London for the Kansas game was 10,518 miles, making it the longest trip of the 2026 NCAA season for any team.

But Dillingham thought his team was mentally prepared for the game.

"I'm still getting a feel for this team," he said. "Every team has different energy. Some are very passionate, emotional. Some, that's not really their deal. I'm getting a better feel for what this team's 'play good' is. But I thought we were fine going into the game. I liked our energy, our focus, our week of practice, and that's the disappointing thing. I gotta figure out why that didn't translate."

There will be a lot of soul-searching after the performance, which also took place in front of a large crowd of high school recruits that ASU brought in. There were a handful of Golden Ticket recipients at the game.

This is one of the lowest points of the Dillingham era since the 2023 season, when the Sun Devils were just trying to hang on with a depleted roster in Dillingham's first season on the job.

"It was an atrocious game," Dillingham said. "We can either point the finger at who was wrong, or we can all take extreme ownership and fix it. The blessing and the curse of it is we've lost games poorly before, and we've bounced back from those games. I think our guys are gonna respond great."

fullText:
Officials in Japan said they lodged a "strong" protest with the United States.

A U.S. service member was arrested on suspicion of murder and robbery after a Japanese woman's body was discovered in a hotel in Okinawa, local officials said, describing the alleged killing as a "heinous" incident that prompted the Japanese government to lodge a protest with the United States.

Shinjiro Koizumi, the Japanese minister of defense, said a U.S. Marine lance corporal was arrested on Sunday after the woman's body was found early on Saturday in Naha, the capital city of the Okinawa prefecture.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the Okinawa Prefectural Police were investigating the incident as a murder.

"The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret, and as the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side," she said on social media.

NHK, Japan's public broadcaster, identified the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, a base a few miles outside Naha. The broadcaster identified the alleged victim as Yagi Anna, 39, saying she was pronounced dead at the scene.

U.S. officials did not immediately confirm the identity of the service member who was arrested, nor did they say whether the person had been officially charged in connection with the death.

"We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force," the force said in a statement on social media. "We extend our deepest condolences to the victim’s family and friends."

Tens of thousands of U.S. troops are stationed across Japan, including in the country's southernmost prefecture, Okinawa, which is home to several U.S. bases.

The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo said it was aware of the incident and was extending "our deepest condolences to the bereaved family of the deceased."

"At present, an investigation is underway to clarify the facts, and the United States Government continues to cooperate closely with the Government of Japan and local authorities," the embassy said in a statement.

George Glass, the U.S. ambassador to Japan, said he had spoken on Sunday morning with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Okinawa's governor, adding that his office was providing full cooperation with an investigation into the death.

title: Raiders Week 4: The Chiefs Las Vegas must stop in key AFC West showdown
description: Patrick Mahomes, Kenneth Walker present quite the challenge for Rob Leonard’s Raiders defense
fullText:
The clash of AFC West unbeatens is set to dominate the afternoon NFL-viewing world this coming Sunday — and for good reason.

The 3-0 Las Vegas Raiders play host to the 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs in an intriguing Week 4 showdown in the desert. The surging Silver & Black led by rookie head coach Klint Kubiak welcome the capable Chiefs captained by veteran Andy Reid in a contest that'll shape up the division just four games into the 2026 campaign.

And, according to 506 Sports, the 1:25 p.m. matchup covers much of the national broadcast map for CBS.

A good old-fashion slugfest is likely on the horizon when the Raiders go toe-to-toe with the incoming Chiefs. Heading into this division tilt, Las Vegas and Kansas City rank fifth and sixth in rushing attempts amongst the 32 teams with only one carry separating the two teams.

It's no secret that Kubiak — the Raiders offensive play caller — alongside his trusted offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko and offensive line coach Rick Dennison love running the football. The 93 rushing attempts is a testament to that. Flip it to Reid alongside his offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy and offensive line boss Andy Heck, and the love for the ground game is equally as feverish. The 92 rushing attempts signifies that.

We established the affinity both the Raiders and Chiefs have for running the ball, but the two squads showcase a balanced offensive attack which makes both difficult to defend.

While they may be in the middle of the NFL pack in passing attempts, Kansas City has thrown the ball 98 times in the trio of games heading into Week 4. Las Vegas, on the other hand, three notches below at 92 total pass attempts on the young season. Comparatively, the Chiefs completed 68.4 percent of the attempts while the Raiders are at 67.4 percent.

So not only will Rob Leonard's Las Vegas defense have to contend with the aerial attack paced by the accomplished Patrick Mahomes, they'll have to deal with his backfield mate, running back Kenneth Walker III — a powerful and elusive ball carrier that Kubiak is all too familiar with as he dialed up plays for Walker when both were Seattle Seahawks last season.

This is the inherent difference between Reid's and Kubiak's ground game: Kansas City has more yards (460) and a larger yards per carry average (5.0), than Las Vegas (300 yards, a paltry 3.2 yards per carry average), in comparison.

Well built at 5-foot-9 and 211 pounds, the 25-year-old Walker has 360 yards on 65 totes and three touchdowns rushing while adding 82 more yards on 11 receptions with a pair of touchdowns. The Michigan State product boasts elite balance, low center of gravity, and explosiveness to evade, elude, and break through would-be tackles. Raiders defenders must be able to wrap up and tackle and when the whiffs come, bank on the team's ability to rally and swarm to the ball.

Walker presents a supreme challenge for the Raiders defense at all three levels and the meeting between the Chiefs tailback and Raiders middle linebacker Nakobe Dean is going to be a powerful one this Sunday.

Rookie safety Treydan Stukes expected return to the starting lineup will help both the run defense and coverage which Mahomes is keen to exploit.

Raiders center Tyler Linderbaum talks about the difficulties the Kansas City Chiefs defense presents & how the O-line is focused on improving the run game this Sunday #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/DaKtLWSodR

While the Chiefs may be light in the sacks department — just three so far — Las Vegas must win the battle at the line of scrimmage. If not, Steve Spagnuolo has the horses on his defense to run circles and lap Kubiak's offense.

Defensive tackle Chris Jones is still a problem — even at age 32. Standing 6-foot-6 and 310 pounds, the Mississippi State product remains a game-wrecker in the middle by collapsing the pocket and neutralizing the pass and run with his veteran savvy and physicality. He's flanked by George Karlaftis and rookie R. Mason Thomas on the edges and both have the strengths and movement skills to mirror against Kubiak's outside/wide zone running scheme.

Behind them are are disruptive linebackers Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill. How that duo reacts and responds to the Raiders' pre-snap motions alongside covering the middle of the field is something to watch. And then there's the secondary featuring cornerbacks L'Jarius Sneed and rookie Mansoor Delane. Both are sticky in coverage adn don't be surprised if Spagnuolo tasks one or both with covering Raiders elite tight end Brock Bowers.

The backend coverage from the secondary and at the second level with the linebackers gives the Chiefs the ability to be sticky and force quarterbacks to hold on to the ball which allows the defensive line to hunt.

Las Vegas offensive line spearheaded by center Tyler Linderbaum and left tackle Kolton Miller will need to be on point to not only open lanes for running backs Ashton Jeanty and speedy rookie Mike Washington Jr. but also keep veteran and statue-esque quarterback Kirk Cousins with a clean pocket and upright.

Las Vegas Raiders QB Kirk Cousins Mahomes Challenge #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/KozIE9Lfqw

Sunday's clash will be the 135th meeting between the longtime AFC West foes. The Chiefs lead the all-time series 76-52-2 (74-55-2 in regular season action, 2-1 in postseason meetings) but it's the Raiders who have the most recent victory — 14-12 this past January. Before that, Kansas City won the last three matchups with a 31-0 win last season being the most lopsided. Dating back to 2016, Las Vegas has won just four times in the 21 meetings.

"I think every week, you're working on your identity, and then someone takes away your identity, takes away something you're good at. So, you got to find multiple ways to win, and that's what good teams do. You got to win on all three phases in order to in order to win, especially against a great team like this."

—Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak when asked about the identity of his football team

"Well, I think he's certainly fun to watch and sets a great standard for quarterback play across our league. And if they were to put up a lot of points, then you got to keep up. You also know that if if you were to get ahead, that no lead is safe. You're just aware of how capable they are any moment of scoring points and making it hard on you as a team. So, there's a lot of respect there, and they've proven it and earned that over many years. And it'll be a great challenge for all of us on Sunday."

—Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins on the challenge Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes presents
