fullText:
CNN has obtained newly unsealed police body camera footage showing the arrest of Luigi Mangione inside a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pennsylvania, days after he fatally shot United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

The hours of footage capture officers questioning Mangione at the fast-food restaurant on the morning of December 9, 2024, before he is handcuffed, searched and transported to the police station. The videos show police conducting more thorough searches of Mangione and his belongings at the station, including the moment an officer finds a gun – now known to be the murder weapon – inside his backpack.

This is the first time the videos have been seen outside the courtroom. Some of the footage was played during a dayslong suppression hearing last December, when the defense argued evidence recovered during the arrest should be suppressed because Mangione’s backpack was improperly searched.

New York State Judge Gregory Carro ultimately ruled most of the evidence would be allowed at trial and placed the videos under seal. The judge authorized their release after CNN petitioned for their unsealing following Mangione’s guilty plea to federal charges in August, in which he admitted to fatally shooting Thompson, 50, on a Manhattan sidewalk.

The unsealed videos, taken from body cameras worn by of eight Altoona police officers, show different angles of how the day unfolded as Mangione was approached and questioned by law enforcement, who quickly came to believe he was the suspect tied to the CEO’s killing.

The footage shows Mangione first provided police with a fake ID bearing the name “Mark Rosario” – the same name prosecutors say the shooting suspect used to check into a New York City hostel prior to Thompson’s killing – before later telling law enforcement his real name.

The officers handcuffed Mangione in the fast-food restaurant and searched his pockets and his belongings, including his black backpack, in which they found a gun magazine wrapped in underwear, the videos show.

Mangione was then transported to the police station, where the videos show both he and his bag were further searched. The footage captures the moments police recovered key evidence from the backpack, including a firearm and a notebook with handwritten entries that prosecutors have described as his “manifesto.”

Mangione’s defense attorneys have asked Judge Carro to dismiss the state murder case against him following his guilty plea in federal court late this summer, arguing he would be unlawfully prosecuted under double jeopardy grounds if it proceeds.

The judge has yet to rule on the motion; the parties are due back in state court in December.

fullText:
A Massachusetts judge has denied Lindsay Clancy's attempt to have the murder charges against her thrown out, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue a retrial in the high-profile case involving the deaths of her three children.

In a ruling issued Thursday, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William F. Sullivan rejected the defense's Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty following September's mistrial. Under Massachusetts law, a Rule 25 motion asks a judge to determine whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to convict.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued the Commonwealth failed to prove two key elements of its case: that Clancy killed her three children and that she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time.

Sullivan disagreed, finding that prosecutors presented enough evidence for a reasonable jury to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy committed the killings and could be held criminally responsible.

“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote.

The decision does not determine guilt or innocence. Rather, it means the judge found the evidence presented during the first trial was legally sufficient for the case to proceed to a new jury.

The ruling represents a victory for prosecutors, who have maintained that Clancy carefully planned the killings of her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on January 24, 2023, then tried to kill herself, while her husband was briefly out of the family's Duxbury home.

Newsweek has contacted Reddington by email and left a message with Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy J. Cruz's office seeking comment.

According to the decision, prosecutors introduced both physical and circumstantial evidence showing that Clancy was alone with the children during the relevant time period. Her husband, Patrick Clancy, testified that he left the house to pick up takeout food and medication and later returned to find evidence of violence inside the home before discovering his children in the basement.

Medical examiners testified that the children died from asphyxia or complications resulting from mechanical asphyxia. Prosecutors alleged the children were strangled with exercise bands.

The judge also rejected the defense's challenge to the state's evidence regarding criminal responsibility. During the trial, both sides agreed that Clancy suffered from a serious mental illness at the time. The central dispute was whether that illness rendered her legally incapable of appreciating the wrongfulness of her conduct or conforming her behavior to the law.

Sullivan noted that three prosecution experts testified that Clancy retained those capacities, even if defense experts reached different conclusions. Resolving those competing opinions, he wrote, is a matter for a jury rather than a judge.

Thursday's decision marks the second time Sullivan has rejected the defense's bid to dismiss the case, finding on both occasions that prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a jury to consider the charges.

“For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge during Tuesday's hearing. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”

A hearing is scheduled for November 2, when the parties are expected to address several unresolved issues, including Clancy's motion to block a retrial on double jeopardy grounds and the defense's request for a court inquiry into Michael Desronvil, the

Defense attorneys have sought scrutiny of Desronvil's phone records as part of their effort to investigate the circumstances surrounding the mistrial and the conduct of the jury's deliberations.

Paul Mauro, an attorney and Fox News contributor, wrote on X after Sullivan's ruling, "Unsurprising. He should similarly swat down the double jeopardy motion and the request to review the holdout juror's phone."

Prosecutors have not yet said whether they intend to retry Clancy. Their options include pursuing another first-degree murder case, seeking lesser charges such as second-degree murder or manslaughter, or declining to move forward altogether.

If a retrial is ordered, a new jury would once again be asked to decide whether Clancy is guilty of murdering her three children or whether her mental state at the time rendered her not criminally responsible.

fullText:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Defense is often the topic when a team is getting set to play at Iowa.

The 14th-ranked Hawkeyes have developed a reputation as a consistent force on that side of the ball, and the 2026 version looks no different through four games for the undefeated Hawkeyes, who host No. 5 Ohio State on Saturday.

Ohio State coach Ryan Day fielded questions about the Iowa defense Tuesday, but he took more about his own stop unit after the Buckeyes allowed 462 total yards, including 199 on the ground, in a 42-19 win over Illinois last Saturday.

That was the high for total yards allowed by Ohio State since Georgia piled up 533 in the 2022 Peach Bowl College Football Playoff semifinal, and the rushing total was the most since Missouri picked up 203 in the Cotton Bowl three years ago.

Perhaps worst of all, the Fighting Illini averaged 6.03 yards per carry, the most by an Ohio State opponent since Michigan averaged 7.2 in 2022.

"Well, I think just coming out of the game, we just have to make sure that we're just executing at a high level across the board in terms of everyone doing their job," Day said. "I think overall you saw effort but just not good enough execution."

While defensive coordinator Matt Patricia dialed up more blitzes and more man coverage than he did in a one-point loss at Texas in Week 2, that also created a need for more discipline that was not always met.

Missed assignments played a role in the Fighting Illini notching seven explosive runs (10 yards or more), equaling the total Ohio State gave up in its first three games combined.

"All it takes is one guy to be out of a gap, and it can turn into an explosive play, so we all have to be disciplined in what we do. We don't just go out there and make plays," Day said. "We have to play within the defensive scheme, but we have to dominate our one-on-one (matchups)."

Senior defensive end Kenyatta Jackson Jr. said allowing nearly 200 yards rushing was "terrible" and "unacceptable."

He also had a term for players not carrying out their assignments: Hero ball, which he described as "not doing your job to the best that you can."

As an example, he mentioned a defensive tackle who is supposed to defend a guard-tackle gap sliding over into a center-guard gap instead, but Jackson also said the fix is easy, something the coaches addressed Sunday after film sessions.

fullText:
Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday for the first time since her murder trial ended with a deadlocked jury.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan for an acquittal, arguing that there was not enough evidence to prove that the 36-year-old former nurse killed her three young children.

"This entire case is based on speculation," Reddington said. "Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this?"

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called the argument "laughable."

Sullivan did not immediately rule. The next hearing in the case is set for Nov. 2.

During the trial, Clancy's attorneys did not dispute that she fatally strangled her children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. She had been charged with three counts of murder in the first degree.

Her lawyers argued that she could not be held criminally responsible for the killings because she was suffering from the rare mental illness that they said made her unable to understand the wrongfulness of her actions.

Prosecutors contended that Clancy, who was never formally diagnosed with postpartum psychosis, carefully planned the killings and bears full responsibility for her children's deaths.

The trial hinged largely on discussions of Clancy's mental state. Over nearly five weeks of testimony, a series of family members and medical professionals took the stand to describe the mental and emotional struggles she endured in the months leading up to the killings.

During deliberations, the 12-member jury informed the judge that the panel was deadlocked: 11 members believed Clancy was not guilty, but one juror refused to apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt, preventing the jury from returning a unanimous not-guilty verdict.

The case finally ended on Sept. 4 following nearly 40 hours of deliberation after the jury came to the judge for a third time to inform him that they were deadlocked, triggering an automatic mistrial under Massachusetts law.

Advocacy groups and researchers said the mistrial highlighted how little the medical field knows about postpartum psychosis, a rare illness estimated to affect one to two per 1,000 women after delivery.

Clancy, who is paralyzed from the waist down since jumping from a second-story window after strangling her children, is expected to remain at a psychiatric hospital where she's been held for the last three years until her case is resolved.

Clancy's attorneys have also asked the judge to dismiss the case on the grounds that the holdout juror should have been removed.

Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to retry Clancy, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters after the hearing. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges, seek to try her on lesser charges, negotiate a plea deal or drop the case altogether.

"We are going to do what we can for the children," Cruz said. "That is what this case is about."

description:

She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
But Reddington told Judge William Sullivan that prosecutors failed to present any evidence at the trial proving she had in fact killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan, saying police conducted a "horrific, ridiculous investigation" that failed to collect evidence showing she killed them.
fullText:
Sept 29 (Reuters) - Lindsay Clancy's lawyers argued on Tuesday that prosecutors had not proven the Massachusetts woman killed her three children in 2023, in a shift from their previous defense that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made that argument during the ‌first hearing in Clancy's case since a judge in Plymouth, Massachusetts, declared a mistrial on September 4 because a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from unanimously ‌deciding whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.

No one at that trial disputed that Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in ​the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.

But Reddington told Judge William Sullivan that prosecutors failed to present any evidence at the trial proving she had in fact killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan, saying police conducted a "horrific, ridiculous investigation" that failed to collect evidence showing she killed them.

"This entire case is based on speculation," Reddington said. "Where is the admission?"

Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham called the argument "laughable" and said it was being raised for the first time at ‌the hearing. During the weeks-long trial, Reddington had instead argued that ⁠Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and did not know what she was doing was wrong.

Reddington also maintained that argument during the hearing, telling Sullivan that every doctor who testified at the trial indicated Clancy was suffering from a serious mental disease or defect at the time.

"The ⁠evidence shows clearly and unequivocally that she was in a state of psychosis," he said.

Buckingham said prosecutors had not disputed that Clancy had mental health issues. But she said the evidence showed that Clancy knew what she was doing and had decided to kill the children after deciding to take her own life.

"She had succumbed to the idea that she didn't want to be here anymore, that she was going to ​commit ​suicide, and that she was going to take those kids with her because no one could care for ​them like she could," Buckingham said.

Sullivan did not immediately rule on the ‌defense's request to declare Clancy not guilty. But he stressed that he did not want the case to linger and told Clancy's attorneys and prosecutors under Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz to be ready to discuss a date for a retrial when they reconvene for another hearing on November 2.

"I think it's important that this case move forward if it has to move forward," Sullivan said.

QUESTIONS REMAIN OVER HOLDOUT JUROR

If convicted on first-degree murder charges, Clancy would face a sentence of life in prison.

Several jurors in televised interviews after the initial trial said that but for the one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.

If found not guilty on those grounds, she ‌would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her commitment would then be subject to regular ​review by the court.

Prosecutors have several options before them, including trying to reach a plea deal or retrying ​Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a ​jury trial and proceed before a judge.

Clancy's lawyers have filed a series of motions seeking to head off the possibility of a retrial and ‌have also asked the judge to conduct a "limited inquiry" concerning the holdout juror.

Sullivan ​said he would take up that issue and ​other motions at the November 2 hearing, as well as a request by prosecutors for a gag order to prevent the "carnival atmosphere" that enveloped her first televised trial and protect the potential jury pool, which they said had been "inevitably tainted."

Prosecutors said the jury pool was polluted as a result of a series of televised interviews in which Reddington ​characterized Clancy as a "wonderful" person, asked President Donald Trump to pardon ‌her, and, "most disturbingly," spoke about the holdout juror "in ways that ensured that juror would be publicly identified."

In a video statement to Fox News' Sean Hannity that aired ​late on Monday, the holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, acknowledged that since the mistrial the focus of attention had shifted to him instead of "on the three angels."

(Reporting ​by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Cynthia Osterman, Bill Berkrot and Deepa Babington)

fullText:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon last week to prioritize and deploy “advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities” to track down, disrupt and neutralize “foreign actors to protect the 2026 midterm elections” while “maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country.”

“Commander U.S. Cyber Command and the Directors of the Combat Support Agencies will prioritize the use of DoW [Department of War] intelligence and cyber capabilities to ensure foreign actors do not meddle in our democratic systems,” Hegseth said in a Sept. 22 memo, which was made public Monday.

The Pentagon chief directed the Defense Intelligence Enterprise to execute collection and production on foreign threats to U.S. elections in accordance with the “law, regulation, Executive direction and DoW policies and directives.”

Hegseth instructed Gen. Joshua Rudd, head of U.S. Cyber Command, to use existing capabilities and authorities in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security to counter “potential cyber threats from foreign actors targeting our elections.”

“Our Nation’s ability to conduct free and fair elections is a steadfast principal of our Democracy,” Hegseth said in the one-page memo. “Assuring and protecting this ability is a no-fail mission and the DoW will do its part in supporting this whole of government effort.”

The meddling of foreign actors and nations has been a concern for U.S. administrations.

Similarly, in 2022, the National Security Agency (NSA) and U.S. Cyber Command under former President Biden highlighted a similar push to safeguard the 2022 midterms from foreign interference and influence.

Rudd told senators during a hearing in January that he would work on safeguarding U.S. elections and protect from foreign interference.

“U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats to our nation. The Command and the Agency regularly counter actions by malicious foreign cyber actors including those with the intent to interfere with our democratic process,” Rudd said in a statement Monday.

title: Major Pentagon breach exposes sensitive data on nearly 3 million people
description:

The breach affected 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 who are deceased, the official said.
fullText:
The breach included Social Security numbers and details about jobs people held.

A breach of the Pentagon’s sprawling personnel database exposed sensitive information belonging to a massive swath of military personnel, including Social Security numbers and details about the jobs they held, according to a U.S. defense official.

The breach affected 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 who are deceased, the official said. The scope and sensitivity of the exposed information could raise national security concerns, particularly because the files included details about the jobs performed by military and civilian personnel.

“A Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) information system experienced unauthorized access of personally identifiable information by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. Upon discovery, DMDC immediately remediated the vulnerability,” the official said.

The Defense Manpower Data Center serves as one of the Pentagon’s main repositories for personnel records, holding information on active-duty and reserve troops, civilian employees, contractors, retirees, veterans and military family members.

The agency maintains more than 60 million personnel records. Military Times first reported the breach last week.

The unauthorized access stretched from October 2025 until July, when DMDC discovered the vulnerability and patched the affected system, according to the defense official, adding there’s no evidence yet that any of the exposed data has been misused.

Defense officials said they have found no evidence so far that the exposed information has been misused and are offering identity protection and credit monitoring resources.

The news of the Pentagon breach comes as the FBI sent a notice to employees on Friday outlining their response to a breach of its jobs portal FBIJobs.gov.

An threat actor said it would publish data including FBI employees' names, home address, personal and work contact information, Social Security numbers, date of birth and emergency contact information, sources told ABC News, and the bureau is operating as if every FBI employee’s personal information was compromised.

But in a statement to the New York Times and 404 Media on Monday, the hacking group shinyhunters claimed it won't release the data as it previously said it would.

"Since the very beginning of this event we have unequivocally and assiduously emphasised this is NOT extortion, this is NOT ransom, this is NOT financially motivated," the statement said. “This was all a marketing campaign to protect our business and actively combat disinformation. If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would’ve never been this widespread."

ABC News has not independently verified the group's claims.

Employees who were impacted have also begun to be notified, and the FBI said that the impacted system -- FBIJobs.gov -- was unclassified.

The FBI also issued a warning for those who might be impacted, advising them to maintain situational awareness and to not answer suspicious calls. There will also be internal briefings for employees who have been impacted.

It also says, according to the warning described to ABC News, that employees should not talk to the media and if the media is "trespassing," employees should call 911.

title: Republicans' frustrations with Hegseth mount as Iran war costs build
description:
The News
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is running into a wall of congressional GOP resistance as he tries to secure $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon next year.
Lawmakers’ growing reluctance to fulfill Hegseth’s eye-popping budget request reflects real intraparty concerns about his leadership, his relationship with Congress, and the ongoing war with Iran. It also punctuates months of drama at the Pentagon over the ouster and resignation of various top officials, in addition to reports of blocked military promotions.
Hegseth’s fraying ties on the Hill put him on course for a bigger headache after the election, according to interviews with a half-dozen senators as well as multiple administration officials.
fullText:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is running into a wall of congressional GOP resistance as he tries to secure $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon next year.

Lawmakers’ growing reluctance to fulfill Hegseth’s eye-popping budget request reflects real intraparty concerns about his leadership, his relationship with Congress, and the ongoing war with Iran. It also punctuates months of drama at the Pentagon over the ouster and resignation of various top officials, in addition to reports of blocked military promotions.

Hegseth’s fraying ties on the Hill put him on course for a bigger headache after the election, according to interviews with a half-dozen senators as well as multiple administration officials.

“This could turn into a real standoff with the military caught in the middle,” a Trump administration official told Semafor. “The implications: There won’t be money available to pay recruitment bonuses, money to upgrade military housing and repair military housing won’t be there, money to fix ships and aircraft from the war won’t be there, and money to restockpile munitions won’t be there.”

“And the longer this drags out, the more dangerous it becomes, because we’re really depleted after the Iran war,” the official added.

Hegseth is pushing for both a sharp increase in military funding — he’s seeking spending more than 40% higher than last year — and a separate $88 billion to cover costs associated with the Iran war and additional weapons. The Pentagon chief’s expansive needs only heighten some Republicans’ skepticism of his leadership over the US military.

It does not appear that Hegseth has an executable plan to get the hundreds of billions in additional military funding he is requesting in the fall, one Republican senator told Semafor, adding that the lack of permanent civilian nominees to lead the Army and Navy are weighing on the Senate. Hegseth’s preferred pick for Army secretary, Sean Parnell, has faced questions over whether he could even be confirmed by the GOP Senate.

“There are a lot of people that are really upset with the war in Iran and how it’s being played out. We feel it’s hurting our chances in the elections in the fall, and it seems rather haphazard,” said the senator.

“We don’t like what we’re seeing when it comes to the pulling of officers off of the promotion lists,” this senator added. “We don’t like what we see with … indiscriminate firings of admirals and generals across the force.”

Hegseth retains the backing of President Donald Trump, despite his Republican doubters in Congress. Those closest to Trump currently see no chance that Hegseth is replaced. That would leave GOP lawmakers with little choice but to work with him, lest they risk holding up funding the White House says is badly needed.

“The president still is very much in Pete’s corner, but beneath him, there are very serious concerns,” the Trump official said. “Are they going to be able to get any additional money through? Are they going to be able to get any nominees confirmed?”

Most Republicans believe a party-line budget reconciliation bill is the best way to get the Pentagon more money after the election. But getting 50 out of the 53 GOP senators on board for that would be a major challenge.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who regrets voting to confirm Hegseth, said the secretary’s quandary “comes down to relationships, and I don’t think he’s built strong enough relationships.” Tillis said the first “meaningful briefing” he’s received on Iran occurred last week; the senator subsequently voted against continuing the war, along with three Republican colleagues.

Those four senators alone would be enough to tank a party-line defense spending bill. And given Hegseth’s distance from Congress, Tillis asked Semafor, “why is anybody going to blindly appropriate anything to him?”

“I agree there’s friction,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “The genesis of that friction is different, depending upon the senator.”

The Trump administration can’t rely on Democrats to pass bipartisan legislation if multiple Republicans are already set to block Hegseth’s request. The secretary, as the administration official noted, is “not going to get Democrat votes — he just can’t do it.”

Kennedy agreed: “Anybody who thinks that we’re going to get money for the Pentagon, which needs it, other than through reconciliation, needs to put down the bong.” He urged Republicans “to sit down and talk about it.”

Hegseth’s supporters also acknowledge a rift that’s damaging the Pentagon’s ability to get what it wants. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an interview that the continued lack of engagement with Democrats “continues to be a strategic error” for Hegseth and his team.

“Republicans are frustrated that he hasn’t reached out to Democrats. He didn’t in his confirmation, and he hasn’t much since at all,” Cramer said.

Kingsley Wilson, a spokesperson for the Pentagon, said the administration conducted over 500 briefings on the budget request — some of them bipartisan — and said the department is “in lockstep with the Republican conference in Congress to achieve the President’s historic investment in defense.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

At the heart of the GOP frustration with Hegseth is his handling of military firings and promotions. Cramer supports much of what the secretary has done but acknowledged the turbulence has “bothered some people.

“And it probably has had an impact on morale a little bit,” Cramer added. “But all in all, I think Pete’s a pretty strong leader.”

Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, worked to arrange a bipartisan classified briefing about the administration’s funding request last week. The Senate Armed Services Committee also heard closed testimony from Hegseth’s top deputies, including Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg.

But Collins is cool to another party-line bill. “I don’t like reconciliation, period,” she told Semafor — and Hegseth, who she voted against.

“One of my concerns, which unfortunately has been borne out, was that he would fire a lot of very capable military officials, and he has done that. He has blocked promotions for some of our most capable military officers,” Collins said. “The number of women and Black people that had been struck from the list was awful.”

“He also is not the most respectful when it comes to Congress’ role,” she added. It’s something Republicans are urging Hegseth to fix.

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., started prodding the Pentagon to go into sell mode last winter. He said he believes the $1.5 trillion top-line number is needed to maintain military superiority but said the administration has got “to communicate that better” to Congress.

“You’ve got to come up here and sell your vision to the board of directors of America, which is us,” Sheehy said. “Everyone has every right to be skeptical … [the Pentagon’s] been almost a symbol of bureaucratic dysfunction. It’s not quite Somali fraud in Minnesota, but it’s been some pretty dumb sh*t we spent money on.”

The upcoming election isn’t necessarily going to bring relief to Hegseth; in fact it might be the opposite, if Republicans lose serious ground in the midterms.

Several of the party’s candidates are now campaigning to end the Iran war, and it’s hard to see where 50 Senate votes for more funding will come from right now. And that’s not even getting into the fractious House.

Trump’s continued backing of Hegseth sets up a choice for Republicans, who have no realistic shot of ousting the defense secretary. They’ll have to decide whether to risk his ire (and military readiness) or hold their nose and vote the money through this year.

Because if Democrats take either chamber of Congress, it appears more military funding is off the table until the war ends.

title: Allen, Bills outlast Chargers 24-16 despite committing 5 turnovers
description: Josh Allen scored two touchdowns rushing and the Buffalo Bills overcame a five-turnover outing to pull out a 24-16 victory over the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday.  Allen’s second score, a 1-yard plunge with 7:35 left, gave Buffalo its first lead.  The Bills then sealed the win on James Cook’s 3-yard run four minutes later, and after Buffalo’s defense forced Justin Herbert's incompletion on fourth down at the Chargers 45.
fullText:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. (AP) — Josh Allen scored two touchdowns rushing and the Buffalo Bills overcame a five-turnover outing to pull out a 24-16 victory over the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday.

Allen's second score, a 1-yard plunge with 7:35 left, gave Buffalo its first lead. The Bills then sealed the win on James Cook's 3-yard run four minutes later, and after Buffalo's defense forced Justin Herbert's incompletion on fourth down at the Chargers 45.

Buffalo improved to 3-0 despite Allen's two interceptions and lost fumble. Cook and tight end Dalton Kincaid also lost fumbles.

The problem for the Chargers was their inability to take advantage — with three of Buffalo's turnovers occurring in Bills' territory.

Los Angeles opened the scoring on Herbert's 1-yard shovel pass to Keaton Mitchell on a drive set up after Cook lost a fumble on Buffalo's first snap from scrimmage. And the Chargers built a 10-0 first-quarter lead on Cameron Dicker's 31-yard field goal that followed Allen's first interception.

For much of the remainder of the game, the Chargers resembled the sputtering offense that opened the season being limited to 14 points per outing and combining for more punts (seven) and turnovers (five) than touchdowns (four) in its first two games.

The 0-3 start is L.A.'s worst since opening the 2017 season with three consecutive losses.

Buffalo, meantime, is 3-0 through three outings for the third straight year and fifth time in nine seasons under Allen.

Allen's two touchdown runs upped his career total from scrimmage to 87 (85 rushing and two receiving) — tying Hall of Famers Thurman Thomas and Andre Reed for the team record.

fullText:
TAIPEI, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The United States "very much" understands Taiwan's defence needs and the severe military threat it faces from China, a senior ‌Taiwanese diplomat said on Sunday, following a Washington summit between the US ‌and Chinese leaders.

Democratically governed Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory, has been waiting for months ​for US President Donald Trump to approve a new arms sales package worth some $14 billion, following up on a record $11 billion deal unveiled last December.

After meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May, Trump said he was keeping the latest arms ‌sales package in abeyance. Trump ⁠has not mentioned the sale since last week's summit, saying only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.

Speaking to ⁠reporters in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi pointed to comments by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that military sales to anyone require the same careful consideration.

"Taiwan ​faces a ​severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even ​though China's economy is declining, ‌it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the US very much understands our defence needs," he said.

Washington also understands Taiwan's determination to invest in its military, Chen added.

"We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the US understands the situation we face and our determination on defence investment completely."

The ‌United States is bound by law to provide ​Taiwan with the means to defend itself. China ​has repeatedly called for military ​sales to end.

David Perdue, the US ambassador to China, told CNBC ‌on Friday that there has been ​no change in Taiwan ​policy by Trump, including on arms sales.

Chen said Taiwan had received confirmation "from our American friends repeatedly that US policy toward Taiwan remains unchanged".

Taiwan's government ​rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying ‌only the island's people can decide their future.

China has rebuffed repeated calls ​for talks by Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, whom it calls a "separatist".

title: Jeremiah Smith and Julian Sayin give Ohio State permission to win differently
description: Maybe Ohio State doesn’t need a historically great defense or a dominant running game this season. Maybe it just needs 20 players to be pretty good, because J.J. and Julian are great enough to handle the rest.
fullText:
For the past two seasons, Ohio State's formula for winning football games has been pretty easy to understand: Have an elite defense, surround it with an offense full of NFL players, and wait for one side or the other to eventually overwhelm whoever is standing across the line of scrimmage. Four games into the 2026 season, however, I think it is becoming increasingly obvious that this team is going to have to win differently.

While very little is objectively bad, at this point in the season, nothing Ohio State is doing right now — offensively or defensively — is even in shouting distance of the level at which Julian Sayin and Jeremiah Smith are playing. And while that is obviously less than ideal, it is certainly not a death knell for the Buckeyes' College Football Playoff aspirations. It just means that the players, coaches, and fans are going to have to adjust their expectations for what winning football is going to have to look like this season.

It would be great if every other position group could somehow become as dominant as Smith and Sayin have been through four games, but I think any objective observer can tell you that that's unlikely to happen this season. Instead, the goal should be for everything else on the team to become reliably good enough to complement Julian and J.J.'s greatness, which is essentially how Ohio State beat Illinois 42-19 on Saturday.

The biggest adjustment that I have struggled to get used to thus far has been with the defense. In each of the past two seasons, the Buckeyes led the country in both scoring and total defense, allowing 12.9 points and 254.6 yards per game in 2024 and a frankly ridiculous 9.3 points and 219.1 yards last year.

At this same point in those seasons — immediately following Ohio State's first Big Ten game — the difference is even more pronounced. In 2024, the Buckeyes were allowing just 196.5 yards and 6.8 points per game. Last season, those numbers were 229.3 and 5.5. Through four games this year, they have ballooned to 274.3 yards and 12.3 points per game. Those numbers are still pretty impressive, don't get me wrong, but not historically so.

After losing an absurd amount of NFL talent over the past two offseasons, perhaps expecting anything else was unfair. I assumed there would be an inevitable reversion to the mean, but I was hoping that the veterans brought in the portal, the experienced players who stuck around Columbus and waited their turn, and the athleticism of the young Buckeyes would be enough to keep the defense amongst the country's best.

Of course, there is still plenty of time for improvement, particularly as young players get more comfortable with their responsibilities, but Saturday illustrated just how far the unit still has to go. Illinois piled up 462 yards, including 199 on the ground and 6.0 yards per carry. Aidan Laughery alone had 113 yards on just 11 attempts. No one with double-digit carries and without a 75-plus-yard run should ever average 10.3 yards per carry against a Buckeye defense.

The defensive line is still searching for the right combination of players, and the linebackers are contributing to the problems against the run. Riley Pettijohn and T.J. Alford have both had moments this season where you can see exactly why the coaching staff is so excited about them, but there were also some substantial assignment failures against Illinois: missing run fits, failing to properly set the edge, over-pursuing ball-carriers, etc.

The secondary has probably been the defense's most consistent unit, yet even there, busted coverages and penalties continue to pop up. So no, this probably isn't going to be a defense that suffocates opponents for 60 minutes every Saturday; it just has to become one that gets enough stops to give Smith and Sayin room to win the game.

The same principle applies offensively. The offensive line was perfectly serviceable against Illinois. Sayin wasn't sacked, and when the pocket did break down, he showed the mobility that we have been waiting to see consistently since his first start. I still think Sayin has room to improve as both a runner and a passer, but his connection with No. 4 has already reached a level of greatness that nothing else on this team even approaches.

On the ground against Illinois, Ohio State ran for 151 yards on 32 carries, which works out to 4.7 yards per carry; serviceable, I suppose, but hardly the type of production that should dictate the identity of the offense.

And I think that is something Ryan Day and Arthur Smith have to accept. Coaches love talking about establishing the run to set up the pass, but with this team, that equation needs to work in reverse. Ohio State needs to establish the pass to set up the run.

Bo Jackson or Ja'Kobi Jackson touched the ball on the first six plays against Illinois, seven of the first eight, and seven of nine on the opening drive. It worked against an overmatched Illini defense, but I am still far from convinced that the Buckeyes' offensive-line personnel and the skill sets of their running backs are enough to change the game against quality opponents.

But the thing is, I don't think they need to be; after all, Jeremiah Smith exists, and he wears scarlet and gray. Illinois inexplicably decided to cover Smith one-on-one far more often than I ever would have considered sane on Saturday, and Sayin punished them for it. Smith finished with career highs of 12 receptions, 217 yards, and four touchdowns, while Sayin threw for 367 yards and four scores without an interception.

J.J. was targeted on nearly half of Julian's 36 pass attempts Saturday. Any time Smith is single-covered, he should be Sayin's first option. Hell, he should probably be his second and third options too. Establish Smith early. Force the defense to abandon whatever machismo convinced it that one defender could handle him. Make safeties shade toward No. 4, make linebackers worry about throwing windows behind them, make defensive coordinators devote an unreasonable percentage of their game plan to one human being. Then let everybody else breathe.

That — combined with Sayin's newfound tough-guy running persona — was essentially the offensive formula I was talking about at halftime on Saturday: Make opponents prove that they can stop the best quarterback-wide receiver connection in college football before voluntarily moving away from it.

That half wasn't perfect for Ohio State, but it just about was for Jeremiah Smith and Julian Sayin. I know Illinois' D is not what it has been under Bert, but this is the type of offense that I want to see. 

A bit of tempo, throw to set up the run, feature 4, Sayin having guts! pic.twitter.com/kFpyEDDY0W

Ohio State doesn't need its running game to become dominant. It doesn't need its defense to replicate the historically great units of the past two seasons. While those things would certainly be nice, it doesn't need every position group to become elite overnight. The Buckeyes just need 20 players on the field to be pretty good, because if they can manage that, Jeremiah Smith and Julian Sayin are great enough to handle the rest.

title: Texas vs Tennessee report card: Arch Manning, offense struggle; defense shines in SEC win
description: How the Texas Longhorns graded out in their 20-17 win over Tennessee. QB Arch Manning and the offense struggle, but Colin Simmons and defense gets high marks
fullText:
Considering the wild ending, Texas football won't soon forget its first trip to Rocky Top.

The No. 1 Longhorns (4-0, 1-0 SEC) opened conference play with a 20-17 win over No. 14 Tennessee (3-1, 0-1) at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn. But the victory came with plenty of anxiety considering the Volunteers scored a touchdown with 1 minute, 22 seconds left in the game and recovered the subsequent onside kick.

But Texas held on for the win and now gets a week break before its annual grudge match Oct 10 against Oklahoma in the Cotton Bowl in Dallas.

Here's how the Longhorns graded out in a 20-17 win over Tennessee.

Arch Manning was more efficient than explosive with 201 yards on 14-of-19 passing. But he didn't toss a touchdown for the first time in the past 10 games and he threw up a prayer to a double-covered Cam Coleman that resulted in an interception. He also absorbed six sacks while failing to get rid of the ball despite decent pass protection. His legs didn't lead to any big plays, but they did lead to two flags for an illegal forward pass.

Hollywood Smothers landed on the injury report all week and missed the game with an undisclosed injury. That meant Raleek Brown carried the load with 67 yards and two touchdowns on 17 carries. Freshman Derrek Cooper had the other seven carries by Texas running backs but tallied just seven yards.

Veteran Ryan Wingo emerged as Manning's most reliable target with six catches for 74 yards. Freshman Jermaine Bishop Jr., the slight but speedy five-star recruit, continues to make more and more of an impact; he had two catches for 34 yards. But where was Cam Coleman? The high-paid portal arrival had just one catch and missed some possessions with an unknown injury.

Sure, Manning holds the ball a long time in the pocket. But the Longhorns did allow a season-high six sacks against a talented Tennessee front. And the line didn't get much push against a questionable Tennessee run defense; the Longhorns averaged just 1.7 yards a carry and totaled 262 yards.

This would have been an A+, but edge rusher Colin Simmons gets docked for his tasteless sack celebration that resulted in a 15-yard penalty and kept a Tennessee drive alive. But Simmons had reasons to celebrate since he tied a school record with five sacks and Texas racked up a total of 10 sacks, which ranks second on the single-game school record list. Tackles Hero Kanu (four tackles, one sack) and Maraad Watson (five tackles, one sack) dominated inside, and end Lance Jackson may just be the most well-rounded defensive lineman on the roster.

Rasheem Biles, a Pittsburgh transfer, continues to make his claim on more All-American honors after a team-high 13 tackles and a late sack that helped seal the win. Justin Cryer (nine tackles) remains a superb sidekick, but the unit does lack depth. Both Biles and Cryer rarely left the field while helping hold Tennessee to 221 yards of offense.

Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon picked on Texas cornerback Bo Mascoe a little bit, drawing two pass interference calls and the late touchdown pass to Mike Matthews. Brandon completed 17 of 29 passes for 145 yards, and the Vols became the first team this season not to turn the ball over against Texas. Texas slot corner Graceson Littleton continues to impress.

Yes, kicker Gianni Spetic made both of his field goals. But those were the only bright spots for a unit that gave up a punt return for a touchdown for the first time in 13 years and failed to cover an onside kick late in the game that could have cost Texas the win. The Longhorns also had an odd illegal fair catch call on Ryan Niblett that wiped out a good return by Bishop.

Defensively, coordinator Will Muschamp produced a brilliant game plan that suffocated a potent Tennessee ground game, which had just 70 yards on 44 carries. Credit head coach and play-caller Steve Sarkisian for sticking with the ground game, but the Longhorns had too many penalties. Texas endured season-highs with 11 penalties for 115 yards, and that ultimately reflects on the coaching staff.

title: Colts' defense has already given up more than 1,000 yards

Broncos defense got back on track in Week 2, but real test comes vs. Rams appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

It's been a tale of two weeks for both the Denver Broncos and the Los Angeles Rams so far in 2026, and now the two collide in Week 3 with both looking to get above .500 for the first time on the young season.

The Rams were humiliated in prime time to open the season in Australia, falling to the 49ers 27-7 in a lifeless performance that was surely affected by their bizarre travel plans. In Week 2, they responded with a dominant 28-6 drubbing of the New York Giants on Monday night to get back to 1-1. Now, it will be a third consecutive prime time game for Sean McVay and company.

The Broncos also took one on the chin in front of the whole nation in Week 1 at the hands of a bitter division rival. But it was how Sean Payton and company responded from that 31-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, with a 20-13 win against the Jacksonville Jaguars, that has fans feeling good heading into the rest of the season.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The story of that turnaround from Week 1 to Week 2 was the Denver defense. Kenneth Walker III ran all over Vance Joseph's unit in the season opener, though it looks like he might do that to just about everyone. In Week 2, the Broncos completely blanked a very good Jaguars offense in the second half and stumped one of the best play-callers in the NFL in Liam Coen.

Now, the Denver defense faces arguably the biggest test in the entire NFL. The Rams have one of the most talented offenses in the league, and even if Puka Nacua isn't able to go because of his hip injury, the combination of Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay makes LA very difficult to stop.

The Broncos slowed down a Jags team that is known for running the ball effectively in Week 2, but they did so mostly by getting to Trevor Lawrence and winning the battle on passing downs. The Jags still had decent success running the ball, gaining 95 yards on 24 carries with an EPA just above zero.

That came on the heels of a Week 1 performance by Denver that was much more alarming in that area. The Chiefs ran for 220 yards with a +0.33 EPA per rush in that game per Next Gen Stats, so the jury is definitely still out on this Broncos run defense.

When you think about the Rams, you think about Stafford, Nacua and Davante Adams, but the running game is the foundation for what McVay wants to do with this offense.

That was on full display in Week 2 on Monday night. The Rams ran for 149 yards on 25 carries against the Giants, to the tune of a whopping +0.36 EPA per play. Both Kyren Williams and Blake Corum are contributing on the ground, and the Rams' offensive line is able to get downhill and dominate in McVay's duo-heavy scheme. If they can do that, Stafford and the passing game will have a much easier time moving the ball as the Broncos pass rush won't be able to pin their ears back.

At the moment, it looks like Nacua is a longshot to play in this game. He was banged up all training camp with hip and groin issues, and didn't practice at all or play in Week 2. He has still yet to practice this week, so his status for Sunday night is looking bleak after McVay called it "doubtful" that he would be out there.

If Nacua doesn't go, that leaves the Rams with Davante Adams as the No. 1 receiver and a host of journeyman options behind him. That didn't hinder the Los Angeles passing attack on Monday night, as Adams reeled in eight passes for 195 yards and two touchdowns. However, this Broncos secondary is a significantly more daunting challenge than the beat-up unit that the Giants rolled out there.

The Broncos love to play man coverage, and they have the personnel to do so with Patrick Surtain II on the outside. Surtain is arguably the best cornerback in all of football and can erase half of the field anytime he is out there.

This season, Denver has played man coverage on 35.9% of its defensive snaps, the sixth-highest number in the NFL according to Football Insights.

Of course, with Nacua likely out this week, Surtain can just follow Adams around all day. That will be especially limiting in the red zone, when the Rams love to get Adams isolated and ask him to win in one-on-one situations.

Behind Surtain, the Broncos still have a number of capable cornerbacks. Riley Moss has become underrated over the years despite being targeted at will, and Ja'Quan McMillian is a quality starter in the nickel.

Behind Adams, with Nacua out of the lineup, Tutu Atwell, Xavier Smith and Konata Mumpfield will all see more looks. Tight ends Terrance Ferguson and Colby Parkinson will also have to step up in this game.

All of these secondary pieces for the Rams will have to make individual plays against the man coverage that the Broncos will throw at them, especially if Surtain is having success against Adams on the outside. Who wins that battle could determine who comes out on top under the lights in Denver on Sunday night.

fullText:
WASHINGTON – Maine Sen. Susan Collins' Republican colleagues swiftly came to her defense the day after the news outlet ProPublica published an investigative story that laid out evidence of alleged involvement in a pay-to-play scheme involving a defense contractor.

The story, which came out on Tuesday, Sept. 22, said that records and emails showed the FBI sought to launch a sweeping investigation examining Collins' interactions with a top donor who won lucrative federal contracts. By late 2024, the agency reportedly had enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe involving Collins and other members of Congress.

But that effort, according to the ProPublica story, evaporated after the Trump administration purged the Justice Department and FBI of its teams that handle public corruption cases.

It's unclear whether the accusations laid out in the article will resonate with Maine voters in November, when Collins is up for reelection in a toss-up race that will prove crucial to whichever party ultimately controls the Senate.

The story does, however, add to a maze of obstacles she's facing to retain her coveted seat in Congress. While she has a track record as a Teflon political candidate in the Pine Tree State, her campaign is already being hurt by an unpopular war, President Trump's trade disputes with Canada and the sudden departure of her initial, scandal-plagued opponent.

Both Collins and her top spokespeople denied any impropriety following the publication of the ProPublica article, saying the Justice Department, dating back to the Biden administration, cleared the senator and her staff of any alleged wrongdoing.

Collins told a Wall Street Journal opinion columnist she was the victim of a "partisan hit job" and questioned why anyone would "take the word of a convicted felon," referring to the defense contractor at the center of the scandal whose cooperation was relied on by investigators to build their case.

"It is so offensive," she said. "This is a smear job."

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told USA TODAY the accusations were a "bunch of BS." Asked why he thought so, he said, "because I know Susan Collins." Cornyn and Collins have served together in the Senate for more than two decades.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Alabama, who sits on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee which Collins leads, argued her Maine colleague has the "utmost ethical standards."

"I have zero concern for any kind of baseless accusations," she told USA TODAY.

Perhaps Collins' quickest – and most politically important – defender was Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

"I don't think there's ever been any implication that she or her campaign were in any way implicated in that," the South Dakota Republican told reporters. "This, to me, looks like a political hit job by a left-wing outlet that's trying to score points going into an election."

Much of Collins' reelection campaign was initially built around fighting Graham Platner, the oyster farmer who eventually dropped out amid a series of sexual misconduct allegations, which he denied. Troy Jackson, a logger and former president of the Maine state Senate, replaced Platner as the Democratic candidate whose name will be on the fall ballot.

In the day since the ProPublica story published, Jackson slammed his opponent over what he called "corruption of the highest order."

"We can’t afford six more years of being sold out to Trump and Collins’ corporate cronies," he wrote in a social media post.

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

fullText:
The Pentagon is altering the promotion process to get to the rank of general in an effort to “cut bureaucracy and demand true meritocracy” across the senior ranks, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Tuesday.

In a video posted to social media, Hegseth declared the Defense Department this year will roll out the Joint Warfighter Evaluation, a new battlefield-style assessment for eligible colonels and Navy captains. The evaluation is intended to screen the officers aimed for one-star general or admiral on “their ability to fight, adapt, and win,” according to Hegseth.

“While the backbone of our military is our NCOs [noncommissioned officers] and our petty officers, victory depends on the commanders who lead them,” Hegseth said in the video.

“America needs warfighters who can master a chaotic battle space,” he added, later noting that commanders should be chosen by “proven competence, not paper credential.”

He likened the new evaluation to the Louisiana Maneuvers — a mass series of military exercises done directly before the U.S. entered World War II, during which roughly 400,000 troops conducted a wargame to evaluate America’s training, logistics and commanders.

Hegseth said such testing brought out leaders like former President Eisenhower, a five-star Army general who planned and carried out the Allied assault on the coast of Normandy and the liberation of Western Europe; Army Gen. Omar Bradley, the first chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who eventually oversaw the U.S. military’s policymaking in the Korean War; and Adm. Chester Nimitz, who commanded Allied air, land and sea in the Pacific theater during World War II.

The Joint Warfighter Evaluation “brings that standard to the modern multi-domain fight,” Hegseth said. “This evaluation is an objective equalizer. The scenario only cares about operational decisions under pressure.”

Hegseth said he had tasked Stuart Scheller, the deputy chief of staff to the undersecretary of Defense for personnel and readiness, to lead the effort a year ago.

Each military branch will have its own version of the evaluation, according to internal documents obtained by The Hill.

The Army will use a written assessment then a digital wargame; the Air Force and Space Force will require a two-hour online analysis test followed by a one-hour interactive simulation; the Navy will have officers travel to the Naval War College for a three-hour written assessment then a two-to-three-hour wargame; and the Marine Corps requires an eight-hour remote evaluation on an AI-enabled platform combining written assessments and situational judgment tests, according to an internal memo.

The Joint Staff will evaluate 50 to 60 Joint Forces Staff College students using a “hybrid” model with an independent written analysis followed by an “in-person, AI enabled execution phase” at Norfolk, Va. school, the memo said.

The current system has promotion boards that consider officers via their accumulated evaluations from their superiors throughout their careers.

The service will provide weekly updates on its pilot program development and implementation of the JWT Operational Planning Team (OPT) that will be coordinated with Scheller, Anthony Tata, the Pentagon’s Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness, said in an Aug. 12 internal memo reviewed by The Hill.

Hegseth, a former Fox News host who served in the Army National Guard, has notoriously had an issue with the military’s promotion system, blocking numerous Army, Navy and Air Force promotions to one-star general or admirals — a large quantity of them Black and female service members.

The Pentagon chief has prioritized what he calls the “warrior ethos,” pushing the armed services to embrace higher physical standards and criticizing the military branches for promoting individuals based on what he has claimed, without proof, are race and gender quotas.

“Real toxic leadership is endangering subordinates with low standards. Real toxic leadership is promoting people based on immutable characteristics or quotas instead of based on merit,” Hegseth told senior military leaders last year in Quantico, Va.

title: Hegseth impeachment fight could put Democrats in a bind after the midterms
description:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.
Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. fullText:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.

Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) defused the issue by punting that vote until after the elections.

But the tides are likely to turn after the election, when Republicans will be freed to weigh in on Hegseth’s fate without fear of a voter backlash, while Democrats will face a tougher choice.

Do they go charging after Hegseth full bore, to appease a liberal base demanding Pentagon accountability? Or do they tread more cautiously, to allow time for the formal investigations many Democrats say they want to see before backing something as explosive as impeachment?

Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, which has jurisdiction over impeachment proceedings, suggested that answering those questions won’t be easy.

“I think that all impeachment articles should be sent to the Judiciary Committee, and we should scrutinize them,” Raskin, a former professor of constitutional law, said last week as Congress was leaving Washington for the long campaign recess.

“I’m not a huge fan of pop-up impeachments,” Raskin continued, “but if that’s all Speaker Johnson leaves us, then we will have to take it very seriously.”

The issue will be an early, postelection test for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who has walked a delicate line under President Trump’s second term as he vies to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

On one hand, Jeffries has faced pressure from the left to fight the president tooth and nail at every turn, no matter the topic. On the other, Jeffries has sought to avoid alienating more moderate voters who are the key to winning battleground districts.

His decision will become even trickier if Democrats flip control of the House, because Jeffries’s ascension to the Speakership will hinge on his ability to win 218 votes on the floor in the first week of January. That task will require the support of all Democrats, from battleground centrists who are cold to aggressive impeachments, to incoming democratic socialists who might view the vote on Hegseth’s removal as a gauge of Jeffries’s leadership credentials.

Jeffries has taken pains to balance those pressures by attacking Hegseth’s track record and calling for his firing while refusing to say if he’ll support impeachment.

“We haven’t ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to us to hold people accountable, and we haven’t ruled anything in. That’s been our position. That will remain our position,” Jeffries told reporters in the Capitol last week.

“Pete Hegseth should’ve never been confirmed. This guy is the most unqualified so-called secretary of war in American history,” he added. “He’s the architect of Operation Epic Failure in Iran that has increased gas prices on everyday Americans and further burdened them economically. … It’s my view that’s the reason why [GOP leaders] pulled the resolution, because there were Republicans who can’t even defend Pete Hegseth at this point.”

The resolution in question, sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), features eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abuses of power related to his handling of the Iran war, a failure to protect civilians and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters, among other charges. Massie introduced the proposal as a privileged resolution, which forces a floor vote even over the objections of GOP leaders.

Johnson evaded that vote by cutting the House calendar a day short last week. But the clock resumes when the House returns on Nov. 9, making Hegseth’s impeachment a first order of business in the lame-duck session.

Democrats have seized on Johnson’s decision, saying Republicans simply feared taking a tough vote ahead of the midterms — an attack that’s allowed them to highlight the unpopular Iran war.

“You talk to Republicans here — which I do a lot, because I’m on the Armed Services and Intel committee — a vast majority of people do not like Pete Hegseth. They think he’s incompetent, at best. They think he’s a clown and a joker at worst. … And a lot of people are somewhere in between,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.). “They don’t want to vote on it.”

Johnson has rejected that narrative as “ridiculous,” saying he simply wanted to grant lawmakers more time to campaign.

But attacking Johnson over the process is different from throwing your weight behind impeachment. Even after the vote was delayed, Democratic leaders distanced themselves from Massie’s resolution and promoted a more deliberative process.

“The DOD mismanagement is incredibly clear, but let’s be honest. The only calls, the only discussions about impeachment in the halls of Congress this week have been from Republicans to impeach Pete Hegseth. No Democratic members were making those calls,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

“We believe in oversight and accountability — that is a hallmark of what this chamber should be doing,” he continued. “We will do that job. We will do it in a thoughtful way.”

Aguilar’s remarks ignored another impeachment push just before the recess, when Democratic Rep. Al Green (Texas) forced a vote to remove Trump over the killing of several civilians by immigration enforcement officers. Many Democrats were furious with Green for distracting from the party’s economic message, and every member of leadership sought to balance competing internal interests by voting “present” — a strategy that could forecast how they’ll approach the Hegseth resolution.

However, heading into that vote, at least one powerful Democrat said Massie has made “very compelling” points about the laws of war and the possibility that Hegseth violated them, which could make it tough for Democrats to do anything but support impeachment.

“He raises a bunch of profound arguments,” Raskin said, “and I’m taking it extremely seriously.”
